    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I swiftly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I swiftly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    According to recent reports, satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software organization, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each new matter at the outset?

    Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of latest datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material problems in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or issue. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    According to recent reports, satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    According to recent reports, ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same plan from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client notes it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    It has been revealed that chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati noted earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely notable, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Recent findings suggest that satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be stated in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

    Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce latest technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.About the Role.

    We’re looking for a Product Manager, Administration & Governance to join our Product Team and make Supabase the default starting point for software built inside a tech giant.

    Sources indicate that supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. Inside most companies, Supabase starts the same way: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. The next step is making that momentum tech giant-wide: one platform where anyone can start building, and where IT can see what’s running, who owns it, and what it costs.

    You’ll own how companies run Supabase as their internal development platform: approved by IT and easy for anyone in the company to use. You’ll make it possible for people and the agents they work with to start building without waiting on infrastructure, while giving platform, IT, and security teams the controls they need to say yes. The goal is to make the approved path the easiest path, from an early experiment to a production application, with the controls companies need built in.

    Own the product strategy and roadmap for internal innovation, from a tech giant’s first IT-approved rollout to adoption across teams and business units.

    Make getting started self-service, whether someone creates a project in Supabase, through an internal developer portal, or with an agent. Give builders the access and infrastructure they need without a ticket for every project.

    Sources indicate that steer scattered usage into a manageable manufacturer-wide platform. Give companies one view of everything they run on Supabase. Shape how ownership, delegated access, and boundaries work so teams can move independently as usage grows.

    In a recent development, partner closely with platform, IT, security, and finance teams to understand what it takes to approve Supabase and keep it approved. Translate their needs into practical identity, policy, audit, and spend controls that don’t slow builders down.

    Define the path from experiment to production, including project ownership, access, and the guardrails that change as an application becomes important to the business.

    Work with Engineering, Design, Sales, and Customer Success to turn early customer rollouts into a repeatable experience, rather than a upcoming custom integration for every manufacturer.

    Define what success looks like, instrument it end to end, and let the data guide what gets built next—from time to first project and self-service adoption to production usage and expansion across the company.

    Have built self-service products that developers love and platform or IT teams trust. You understand both the person trying to ship an app and the team responsible for how it runs.

    Can reason about identity, permissions, organization boundaries, and usage attribution, and turn those systems into workflows people can actually understand.

    Have a strong point of view on how agents change who can build software inside a company and what an internal development platform needs to make that possible.

    Know your way around controlled experimentation and data analysis, and can connect easier adoption to sustained product use.

    Are biased toward speed and would rather ship, learn, and iterate than perfect a spec.

    Build with what you own and form opinions through first-hand use, from creating a project to configuring the policies around it.

    Use AI tools to compress research, drafting, and feedback synthesis so you can focus on judgment calls.

    Work async by default, making decisions in writing in a fully remote team.

    In a recent development, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    In a recent development, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    After Weil Gotshal’s collapse, law firm merger interest heats up

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Recent findings suggest that consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both stated they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both mentioned they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

    Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s vital to look at their options early.”.

    #136834. Tech Report: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1331 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • Sources indicate that iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • Industry observers note that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is right now considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    Sources indicate that iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    Industry observers note that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    In two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    Industry observers note that in addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Recent findings suggest that within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Recent findings suggest that last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    It has been revealed that the solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    According to recent reports, but the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    Industry observers note that once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

    Tech Report: 2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before.
    • Industry observers note that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors.
    • It has been revealed that it was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

    Industry observers note that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

    It has been revealed that it was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

    It has been revealed that trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize plans and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

    It has been revealed that AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect users and the public at large.

    Recent findings suggest that at Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate newly introduced AI-driven workflows into their firms.

    Drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report demonstrates that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

    The growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a new category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

    Industry observers note that as AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow users to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

    Industry observers note that partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were new products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

    Recent findings suggest that litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

    It has been revealed that as newly introduced AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to rapidly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

    Nicole Black is a Rochester, Fresh York-based attorney, author and journalist. She is the principal legal insight strategist at 8am, parent organization of LawPay, MyCase, CasePeer and DocketWise. She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association. She writes regular columns for ABAJournal.com and Above the Law, has authored hundreds of articles for other publications, and she regularly speaks at conferences regarding the intersection of law and emerging technologies. Follow her on LinkedIn, or she can be reached at [email protected].

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    #136831. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1583 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent upcoming book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent upcoming book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history highlights that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    According to recent reports, shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    Recent findings suggest that but this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    Chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    Marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    It has been revealed that justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    In a recent development, nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political complications as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    According to recent reports, and in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Newly introduced York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Upcoming York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Industry observers note that justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to issue a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a newly introduced story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    Industry observers note that if I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    Not Horsing Around: Carriage owners file lawsuit to challenge fresh ban in NYC

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A recent Fresh York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.
    • A recent Upcoming York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.
    • The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A recent Fresh York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent Upcoming York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani aims to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Additionally, the latest law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani stated.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    • A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.
    • Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department).

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    Prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video demonstrates him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

    #136822. Five major concerns that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2629 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Five major concerns that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • Before we explore some of the major complications pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile complications as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    Before we explore some of the major complications pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    According to recent reports, litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    After a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the concern, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    Once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court introduces in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    According to recent reports, the court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    For a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely announces that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    Recent findings suggest that once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile issues that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    One week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    This ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    Recent findings suggest that shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either at the moment serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    In March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    Sources indicate that U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    Sources indicate that on Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    Recent findings suggest that as expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    This week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    Nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    Last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the issue will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    In addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    In a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    Industry observers note that because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    Industry observers note that as I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration issues dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    Industry observers note that and there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    It has been revealed that suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    The responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    The rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    Several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are currently considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, New Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the company. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    The responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    In its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to matter universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    After CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    The case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    That deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    The justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    November 23, 2026, 10:03 am CST.

    In an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 fresh federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations. (Image from Shutterstock).

    In an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 new federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations.

    Congress last enacted a significant expansion of the federal courts in 1990, according to a story by Law360.

    The federal courts presently have 677 district judgeships and 179 appellate judgeships. Under the bill, judgeships would be added in a number of states, including Arizona, California, Iowa, Newly introduced Jersey and New York.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a version of the bill in 2024, but then-President Joe Biden vetoed it during his last few weeks in office.
