    #136734. Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1870 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding.
    • The plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system.
    • Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at issue clearly authorizes them.

    The plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit considered Crowther’s and Joseph’s cases together. It held that Title IX does not provide a right – either explicitly or by implication – for employees to sue for sex discrimination. When the full court declined to reconsider their case, Crowther and Joseph asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which it agreed in May to do.

    In a recent development, crowther and Joseph urge the justices to reverse the 11th Circuit’s decision and allow their lawsuits to go forward. They point to the text of Title IX, which provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” That language, they say, creates a broad ban on sex discrimination by schools that receive federal funding; moreover, they add, Title IX “also contains ‘a list of narrow exceptions’ that does not include employment discrimination” – further evidence that Congress intended Title IX’s ban on sex discrimination to apply to both employees and students.

    In a recent development, the Georgia university system agrees that Title IX bars sex discrimination in employment, “and that federal agencies may deny funding to violators.” But that is not the question before the court, it stresses. Instead, it emphasizes, the matter is whether Title IX allows employees to bring private lawsuits alleging that they were the victims of sex-based discrimination. The answer, the university system notes, is no.

    Industry observers note that to support their position, Crowther and Joseph cite several past Supreme Court rulings, including its 1982 decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell. In Bell, the court upheld regulations, meant to implement Title IX, that barred sex-based discrimination against employees (as well as students) at federally funded educational institutions. That decision, they say, demonstrates that Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in employment. “The Court’s cases, read together,” they continue, “lead to the inexorable conclusion that an employee who is a victim of intentional sex-based discrimination by a federally funded education program or activity has a private right of action to seek damages under Title IX.”.

    It has been revealed that crowther and Joseph add that the Supreme Court has allowed employment discrimination lawsuits under other federal antidiscrimination statutes that apply to the recipients of federal funds – Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits discrimination based on disability. Those laws, they write, contain “virtually identical” language – further evidence that Title IX allows lawsuits like theirs.

    The university pushes back against the employees’ attempt to draw comparisons with other federal antidiscrimination laws. It writes that Supreme Court “has assumed,” but has never specifically held, that “Title VI permits private suits for the narrow category of employment discrimination that statute prohibits.” But in any event, it notes, that assumption does not indicate anything about whether Congress created a private remedy in Title IX. The university system also emphasizes that “[t]he Rehabilitation Act has always been a far more detailed and targeted statute than Title IX” – for example, it “expressly ban[s] disability discrimination by the federal government as [an] employer.”.

    Similarly, the university system continues, the Supreme Court’s decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell does not resolve the question before the justices now. The court in that case, it writes, “had no reason to, and did not, consider whether Congress created a private remedy atop the express one the challenged regulations implemented.”.

    Whether the availability of another remedy forecloses private lawsuits under Title IX.

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court, the university system writes, has made clear that the right to bring a private lawsuit hinges on whether there is “evidence confirming that Congress sought to” provide such a right. And when Congress has created “an express remedy” in another statute, there is “a strong ‘presumption’ that Congress did not imply others” – particularly when that “express remedy” involves a “‘comprehensive’ remedial scheme.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that is exactly what happened here, the university system argues. “Mere weeks before Congress passed Title IX,” the university contends, “it extended … [the] protection—and reticulated enforcement scheme” in Title VII to school employees, which bars employment discrimination based on (among other things) sex. Therefore, the university system notes, allowing lawsuits like Crowther’s and Joseph’s to go forward under Title IX “would attribute to the same Congress an inexplicable about-face: Immediately after giving a set of employees a private employment-discrimination remedy mediated by a ‘detailed administrative and judicial process,’ it silently gave the same employees a second private right of action, to attack the same basic harm.” And it did so, the university system suggests, without requiring employees to comply with any of the “strings attached” to private lawsuits under Title VII – including, but not limited to, the requirement to first file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before going to court and its limits on the damages that can be recovered.

    Crowther and Joseph counter that “Title IX and Title VII are ‘vastly different.’” The prospect “that an employee might be able to bring a claim under both Title IX and Title VII does not justify” a determination that a private right of action is not available under Title IX. Rather, they write, the Supreme Court “has recognized that Congress has enacted overlapping remedies to eradicate employment discrimination, and Congress chose not to exclude employment discrimination from Title IX’s broad reach.”.

    Sources indicate that as additional support for the idea that Title IX does not provide a private right of action for employees, the university system notes that the law was enacted pursuant to Congress’ power under the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which gives Congress the power to impose taxes and spend money for (among other things) the country’s “general welfare.” In exchange for the federal funds, the recipients therefore agree to comply with the conditions that Congress imposes, and Congress can terminate the funding if a recipient fails to do so. However, in cases such as last term’s Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, the Supreme Court has held that additional sanctions for violating the conditions in a law, such as the ability to bring a private lawsuit, are only available if the recipient has knowingly and voluntarily agreed to those sanctions. Here, the university system asserts, “Title IX does not unambiguously authorize private employment-discrimination suits,” and so it could not have known that it could be sued by employees, much less have agreed to that possibility.

    Crowther and Joseph reject this argument. They say that recipients of Title IX funds “‘have been on notice that they could be subjected to private suits for intentional sex discrimination under Title IX since 1979.’” As a result, they write, the Supreme Court’s “Spending Clause precedents ‘do[] not preclude private suits for intentional acts that clearly violate Title IX.’”.

    A “friend of the court” brief from West Virginia and 20 other states attempts to refute this assertion. The states tell the justices that the states “are best positioned to say what Title IX’s bargain contains, as they’re the ones who’ve accepted it.” And they “can say with firsthand authority that the deal they made did not include this,” they write. “To the contrary, all the circumstances suggested to the States that Title VII [procedures, not private lawsuits] was the rightful home for those cases.”.

    The Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting the university system, urges the justices not to reach the Spending Clause question at all. Instead, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the justices, they “should decide this case on the ground that” the employees’ “claims fail as a matter of ‘statutory interpretation’ alone.” Therefore, he writes, it is “unnecessary to reach, and prudent to avoid, the parties’ further dispute over the constitutional notice requirement for legislation enacted under Congress’s spending power.”.

    The possible effects of the court’s decision.

    Sources indicate that both the Trump administration and lawyers representing public school districts warn that a ruling in the employees’ favor could have “significant adverse consequences.” The federal government suggests that allowing lawsuits like the employees’ to go forward “would crowd judicial dockets with premature lawsuits that could often be avoided through proper use of Title VII’s administrative process, which successfully resolves numerous cases. And it would undermine the government’s primary authority to enforce both Title VII … and Title IX.”.

    In a recent development, for its part, the National School Attorneys Association emphasizes that “public school districts typically operate with limited legal and administrative staff. Expanding Title IX’s implied private right of action to cover claims against employees,” it notes, “would impose disproportionate compliance and litigation burdens on public school districts and diminish the limited resources they have to educate students.”.

    But a brief from the National Education Association, supporting the employees, takes a contrary stance. It tells the justices that upholding the 11th Circuit’s decision “would remove a critical deterrent against sex-based mistreatment of educators, exacerbate an already dire workforce crisis, and ultimately compromise the quality of education available to millions of students nationwide.” Lawsuits under Title VII, it writes, are not enough because that law “does not offer the full protections to which employees of education programs are entitled.”.

    A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for people’ downtime?
    • People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for people’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help customers pass the time.

    AppLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    It has been revealed that now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s upcoming Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Industry observers note that some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    But, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    The Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Sources indicate that bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    Sources indicate that but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    But there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-new businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Industry observers note that will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    Sources indicate that the Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)

    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    According to recent reports, so what changed? TTD latched onto a upcoming principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the firm built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    Sources indicate that as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    It has been revealed that if The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a fresh era for the organization:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The tech giant should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    Industry observers note that 3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    From the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data stated it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the tech giant’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    The business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    In 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    Recent findings suggest that redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    According to recent reports, advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    Recent findings suggest that the concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    According to recent reports, television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    Advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    Industry observers note that none of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only company in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    In a recent development, most turnarounds require a company to find a new reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    #136727. AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (681 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
    • Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
    • At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

    Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

    At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

    Indeed, it’s the crux of the company name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

    In September, it launched its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

    Sources indicate that stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” said Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

    Coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

    For this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” mentioned Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

    Industry observers note that based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène noted. It then validated the decision by testing the new designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

    But rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, said Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

    Recent findings suggest that when your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

    But no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, stated Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

    An AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” said Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

    Stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell consumers what they want to hear, said Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

    Industry observers note that having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène said. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.
    • So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.
    • The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

    So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

    The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

    The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

    Other changes to the documentation are less important, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

    Marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search owners. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

    Plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently introduced “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

    It has been revealed that but AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

    Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

    Industry observers note that all that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

    Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

    It’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for users.

    Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

    Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research says that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

    It has been revealed that ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

    Industry observers note that while the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

    Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

    According to recent reports, would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

    Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

    Microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

    In a recent development, after Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the firm has appointed its newly introduced CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

    According to recent reports, agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

    Recent findings suggest that CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].

    #136722. Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (506 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.
    • It’s a head-scratcher, states Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.
    • “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he notes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.

    It’s a head-scratcher, states Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.

    “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he notes.

    In a principal media deal, an agency isn’t just advising a client; it’s selling to them. The agency buys media in bulk with its own money, then resells it to the client – usually without saying what’s in the package or what it paid – and then keeps the difference.

    Which raises an obvious question: Is the agency recommending what’s best for its client or what’s best for the agency?

    To understand how the industry got here, Asghar says, you have to go back around 25 years to when media buying was unbundled at the behest of procurement and agencies started pooling client dollars to gain leverage. The original idea was to pass along the savings.

    But after the ANA’s K2 report came out in 2016, it became clear that agencies were holding onto big volume rebates for themselves.

    “They’re not actually savings; they’re profit,” Asghar says. “And they’re about the purest form of profit a company could attribute to their bottom line.”.

    Today, holding companies have repackaged those rebates as principal deals, which is really just arbitrage. Asghar argues that this money should go back to the client.

    According to recent reports, not that any of this is happening secretly, though. Defenders of principal media like to say it’s fine as long as clients opt in. But Asghar isn’t buying it.

    “It’s one thing to know it’s happening,” he notes. “It’s another thing to know what’s happening inside of what’s happening.”.

    Sources indicate that in other words, marketers can sign off on a principal deal and still have no idea what ended up on the plan. They often can’t get log-level data showing where their ads ran or what they originally cost. And because agencies buy the inventory at undisclosed discounts or through volume rebates before reselling it at a markup, the true price is hidden.

    Marketers should go back to buying media separately from planning and strategy services, Asghar indicates, so the agencies giving advice aren’t also the ones with inventory to move.

    Otherwise, Asghar claims, an agency isn’t really acting as an agent.

    Being a fiduciary, he says, “means you have a responsibility to do what’s in the best interest of [clients], not just what’s in the best interest of you or your shareholders.”.

    Also in this episode: Why AI is going to “make dumb companies dumber and smart companies exceptional,” why young planners still need to learn the old-fashioned way even if agents can do some of their work for them and why attribution and measurement are the “dry turkey” of ad tech. (It “looks great on the outside,” Asghar quips, “but it’s terrible on the inside.”).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When OpenAI declared in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.

    But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.

    On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, announced its ChatGPT ads offering.

    According to recent reports, webMD Ignite serves hospitals and healthcare providers with agency solutions as well as content and data solutions, including its own DSP. Now, its agency offerings will include the opportunity to launch ads in ChatGPT.

    ChatGPT Ads’ most recent ad policies provide more explicit detail on what is and isn’t permitted within healthcare advertising and offer more leeway than before. At least, there’s more leeway in the US – heath-related ads are still “generally prohibited” in other countries, according to the policy.

    The ad policy also states that regulated products and services are still prohibited writ large, as are “claims related to the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of physical or mental health conditions.”.

    However, OpenAI may accept ads on a case-by-case basis for less regulated offerings, including hospital and urgent care, health insurance, dietary supplements and consumer medical devices, wearables and apps.

    Of WebMD Ignite’s clients, OpenAI has thus far only permitted ads from health systems and providers (like hospitals and academic medical centers), but not insurance companies.

    In a recent development, over 30% of Americans have used AI chatbots for health advice or information, so medical providers want to ensure that they’re “present and discoverable” within LLMs, said Ann Bilyew, president of WebMD Ignite. Ads are a seemingly straightforward way to achieve that presence.

    According to recent reports, the problem, mentioned Bilyew, is that most of them aren’t sure how best to design the creative and messaging in a way that will let them through the “gates” of OpenAI. WebMD Ignite works directly with OpenAI, and so has more insight into the protocol and standards. “As we learn something for one health system, we’re able to apply it to all the others,” said Bilyew.

    It’s too early to assert any definitive learnings, but WebMD Ignite believes that “contextual alignment will be a critical driver of performance,” Nora Simmons, VP of activation strategy, told AdExchanger.

    ChatGPT has a “relatively constrained creative format” that, for the moment, consists of an image, the brand name and a brief message, said Simmons, and doesn’t allow for particularly unique ad formats. As a result, she said, it’s particularly important to ensure that the ad’s message – and then the landing page, if a user clicks on the ad – matches the intent of the user’s conversation.

    It has been revealed that it’s also crucial that the ad is “informational, not promotional,” noted Bilyew – though she acknowledged that the line between the two can be quite blurry. Generally speaking, informational ads can include specific examples of the services offered, locations and any certifications and awards they’ve received.

    Healthcare marketers also aren’t immune to the challenges that all ChatGPT advertisers face: namely, knowing what sort of queries their ads appear against.

    In a recent development, clients can see data on views and clicks, noted Bilyew, but not on the specific content (or even types of content) that their ads appear next to. This is particularly challenging for healthcare advertisers, since ads are prohibited from appearing in any health-related conversations that are deemed sensitive or personal, making it more difficult to predict what queries they can show up against.

    Determining what makes a conversation too sensitive for advertising is a subjective metric, but OpenAI told AdExchanger that even if a health condition is “strongly implied,” rather than explicitly stated, ads won’t be served during the conversation. “Someone does not need to explicitly name a diagnosis or ask for medical treatment for a conversation to fall into that sensitive category,” remarked OpenAI.

    For now, WebMD Ignite is optimizing its clients’ ads for informative content that doesn’t directly refer to the user’s own health conditions, such as queries like, “I’m looking to understand heart health,” said Bilyew.

    WebMD Ignite also needs to have different versions of an ad for different contexts. For instance, Simmons mentioned, a cardiology center would want to offer different messaging to someone looking to find a cardiologist versus someone asking specific questions about a particular cardiac procedure. It’s been testing roughly 100 creative variations in its early work with the cardiology division of an academic medical center, with “different messages, conversational contexts and geographic markets,” she added.

    It has been revealed that but one of WebMD Ignite’s greatest strengths is its willingness to admit how little is known about AI search advertising at this early stage. “We don’t know what a good budget should be in a given region,” said Bilyew, or what the delivery or inventory will look like. “We’re starting with very defined tests,” she added, and comparing the results to paid search to start assessing budget allocation on a larger scale.

    It has been revealed that “Our message to clients is, ‘Look, just get in there and start learning,’” Bilyew said. “Then, as things evolve, you’ll be in a good position to evolve with it.”.

    Amazon Can’t Quit ChatGPT; Manipulative Mobile Game Ads Win

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday.
    • Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.
    • In a recent development, the two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Happy Thanksgiving! The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday. The Daily News Roundup will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

    Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.

    In a recent development, the two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media. But they also can’t completely cut each other off from their respective platforms without threatening potential sales.

    The retail media model, which Amazon has perfected, works because it’s easy to connect ads to purchases, Shields writes. But when chatbot-based research becomes part of the customer journey, the path from ad exposure to final transaction gets much harder to trace. Just look at the IAB’s new convoluted AI attribution framework, which does what it can to try and account for the many ways AI can influence a purchase.

    Meanwhile, Amazon realizes OpenAI is trying to steal its lunch. That’s why Amazon blocks OpenAI crawlers from accessing its retail site and prevents ChatGPT ads from linking directly to Amazon product listings.

    But not even Amazon could resist the urge to advertise on ChatGPT during the holiday shopping season, Digiday reports.

    That creates an awkward situation for Amazon, however. Its restrictions on OpenAI are also impacting how its own ad attribution works. For instance, Amazon’s ChatGPT ads direct shoppers to complete their purchase on Amazon’s site. But because they can’t click through to the product page, they have to click through to search results instead.

    And, because OpenAI can’t scrape Amazon’s site or its product pages directly, ChatGPT has to analyze info sourced from third-party deal-tracking sites to give shoppers useful advice.

    Good luck to the measurement platforms trying to make any sense of all this!

    Recent findings suggest that most readers may not recognize the mobile game Gossip Harbor. But its social and mobile video ads are hard to miss: horrific AI-generated scenes of marital infidelity, child neglect and animal abuse, alongside strange calls-to-action involving scenes like a mother and daughter freezing in a collapsing shelter.

    According to recent reports, the trend of AI-generated crisis ads has been covered at length, and there’s a whole economy of mobile games that redirect the resulting traffic to unrelated titles. It sounds like an implausible business model – but the numbers tell a different story.

    According to recent reports, sensor Tower and GameRefinery data show Gossip Harbor climbing the revenue rankings in Apple’s App Store and Google Play this year. By November, its monthly in-app revenue had topped even Candy Crush’s roughly $100 million. Mobile growth consultant Matej Lancaric has a blog post detailing the game’s revenue and marketing strategy.

    Aside from its ghastly creative approach, Gossip Harbor is one of the biggest games in the mobile category. What is that, you might ask? In many popular mobile merge games, players keep progressing through an ongoing story on a persistent board instead of clearing one level after another. The game is designed to go on indefinitely with regular updates.

    The ads prey on people’s anxiety to attract players, and then the games monetize the attention that follows.

    Black Friday deals just don’t hit the same way they once did – and not only because fewer people are willing to get into parking lot fistfights over them.

    In a recent development, part of the problem, Marketing Brew argues, is that the savings are no longer relegated to a single day. Extending Black Friday into an entire month not only eases the fear of missing out, but also creates something called “promotion fatigue,” where customers are unsure about the right time to buy and may end up buying less as a result.

    On top of the constant deals, customers have also become generally less trusting that they’re actually getting a bargain during the holiday season. Which makes sense because, oftentimes, they’re not.

    In a recent development, as watchdog group Groundwork Collective recently found, some retailers advertise Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals that don’t offer any significant savings. Others, meanwhile, reserve cheaper, lower-quality inventory specifically to sell during Black Friday, especially electronics.

    So how should advertisers approach Black Friday shopping campaigns? Well, actually making the deals worthwhile would go a long way, for starters. For some companies, that might include staggering which products go on sale and when or ensuring that the prices are meaningfully low.

    Or you could just forgo the Black Friday rhetoric entirely and focus on brand-building instead, of course.

    Recent findings suggest that tidal bans AI-generated music from its platform entirely and will remove 29 million AI songs, claiming that 96% of AI tracks receive zero plays. Tidal already demonetized all AI-generated songs five months ago. [Variety].

    During an all-hands meeting discussing his comeback, returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang claims the company will hire a compliance officer “for the first time.” [post].

    Industry observers note that private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners has finalized its purchase of a majority stake in Puck, a digital news publisher. [The Wrap].

    Writer, podcaster and events host Alex Konrad is making his small media business work by focusing on startup founders and ventures. [Inc.].

    What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.
    • Sources indicate that but what does performance actually mean in TV environments?
    • According to recent reports, these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in Latest York City on Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.

    Sources indicate that but what does performance actually mean in TV environments? And what do media buyers need to achieve that performance?

    According to recent reports, these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in Latest York City on Thursday. Go Addressable is a nonprofit trade organization focused on advancing addressable TV advertising.

    According to recent reports, different advertisers typically have their own metrics for defining performance, ranging from reach and brand awareness to purchase consideration and real-life sales. But what buyers agree on is the belief that brand awareness and performance are not only connected, but causal.

    When it comes to TV and video ads, “if we don’t have scalable audiences, we can’t drive outcomes,” said Maureen Bosetti, chief investment officer at Omnicom Media Group, speaking on a panel taking place on the Go Addressable stage.

    In other words: The entirety of the marketing funnel matters when running TV ads that aim to move money – not just lower-funnel numbers like retail sales. Hence the renewed prevalence of the term “full-funnel” in TV advertising discussions, including during this year’s upfront season.

    Improved measurement and transparency are at the top of buyers’ wish lists to help make TV ads work as desired. Hopefully publishers and their intermediaries will listen this time.

    When it comes to measuring video ad outcomes, the TV industry is setting itself up for disappointment because we “oversimplify” the human nature of viewers, said Jennifer Gardner, chief client solutions officer at Carat US, a subsidiary of dentsu, speaking on the same panel.

    No matter how many QR codes and calls to action advertisers slap onto ad creatives, TV is still a lean-back viewing environment. At least compared with other channels and personal devices used for online shopping, such as cell phones, laptops and tablets.

    Generally speaking, TV viewers are not going to immediately pick up their phones or pause their show to run to the store when they see a commercial advertising an interesting product, Gardner stated. More often than not, viewers store that information to look into later, when they’re not in the middle of the show.

    Seeing a brand’s advertised product in the wild over time also plays a role in persuading viewers to buy something they remember seeing on TV, Gardner added. “Purchase behavior is heavily influenced by mindset,” she said, “which is built over time.”.

    Sources indicate that plus, performance encompasses more than just sales. Different category verticals have their own preferred outcomes they use to gauge performance.

    It has been revealed that for example, fast-food and quick-service restaurants (QSR) often prioritize incremental reach as their preferred metric of performance, Bosetti stated. For QSR brands, reach drives foot traffic, which drives business, she said, noting that QSR brands often plan media based on channels and platform most likely to reach, say, households with young children who frequent fast-food restaurants multiple times per week.

    In other words, Bosetti said, an upper-funnel play can also be a performance-driven one.

    Despite the variances in how brands define outcomes – and how long it takes for TV to have an impact on driving those outcomes – agencies agree they need better measurement and transparency.

    Conversations pushing for better measurement and transparency have been ongoing for multiple grueling years (can confirm). Years of demands and effort toward that pursuit have led to a renewed rise in marketing mix modeling (MMM) and piecemeal upgrades in content transparency across certain publishers and their tech partners.

    According to recent reports, upgrades are cool. But according to agencies, they’re not enough.

    MMM is valuable, Gardner mentioned, but it is “backward-looking” and “doesn’t tell you about changes happening in the future,” which makes it difficult for marketers to use insights from MMM before it’s too late.

    Agencies need more than just MMM to measure and optimize campaigns.

    What agencies need, Bosetti stated, is standardized and “holistic” measurement that gives buyers a comprehensive view of customers and their consumption behaviors across channels, from broadcast TV and streaming to social media and online video. That comprehensive view, she said, is a core component to agencies’ ability to spot opportunities for cost-cutting and improved ad effectiveness.

    Transparency is also an crucial part of the ad measurement equation.

    Industry observers note that A lot of media plans have “dead reach,” Gardner stated, which agencies can mitigate if they have a better understanding of their target consumers. That comprehensive understanding goes beyond just audience signals and identity resolution, though, she said. According to Gardner, agencies need more detailed data from sell-side partners that capture content signals and attention data.

    Agencies want publishers to cough up more information about what viewers are actually watching and what they’re paying most attention to.

    But will they? Won’t they? Or will more debates over measurement and transparency continue to be the object of a tug-of-war game between agencies and publishers?

    Only time will tell, but don’t worry – we’re keeping close watch on this space.

    #136706. Senior Product Marketing Manager at Kit

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1750 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realworkfromanywhere ↗ Open Full Page

    Senior Product Marketing Manager at Kit

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve.
    • It has been revealed that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    It has been revealed that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    Sources indicate that you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, launches, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing currently works at Kit.

    Sources indicate that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action proposal on how we can win these creators.

    It has been revealed that first Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a newly introduced tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth manufacturer, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    Sources indicate that you lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    You work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Industry observers note that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Recent findings suggest that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    It has been revealed that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance looks through Aetna.

    Industry observers note that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Manufacturer-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    In a recent development, we value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.
